column1: What is the single critical condition (the 'shear line invariant') that must be satisfied for a pin tumbler plug to rotate?
column2: Every pin stack's key pin/driver pin break point must align exactly at the shear line simultaneously, so no metal crosses the boundary between plug and shell.

column1: In a pin tumbler lock, what two components make up each pin stack, and which one must stay above the shear line while the other sits at/below it for the lock to open?
column2: The key pin (lower, contacts the key) and the driver pin (upper, contacts the spring). The driver pin must stay above the shear line while the key pin rests at the shear line.

column1: Why is picking impossible in a theoretically 'perfect' lock with zero manufacturing tolerance?
column2: With zero positional/diameter variance, all driver pins would bear against the cylinder wall simultaneously under torque, so the plug could not rotate even fractionally without shearing all pins at once—eliminating any sequential binding order to exploit.

column1: What causes one specific pin to 'bind' first when tension is applied to a plug?
column2: Manufacturing tolerances (~±0.015–0.030 mm) mean pin chambers are never perfectly concentric; the chamber with the greatest radial offset contacts/binds against its housing channel edge first under rotational torque.

column1: Describe the sequential feedback loop of single-pin picking after a binding pin is set.
column2: Lifting the binding pin to the shear line lets the plug rotate a tiny angle (~0.02°), trapping the driver pin above the shear line (an audible/tactile 'click'). This shifts rotational load to the next most-misaligned pin, repeating until all pins are set.

column1: What happens mechanically when a spool or serrated security pin is lifted during picking, causing a 'false set'?
column2: The pin's waist/serration catches at a false shear line position, causing the plug to rotate further than normal into a false-set; as the pin's narrow waist clears, the tension wrench feels counter-rotation (reverse torque) before the true set is reached.

column1: Without tension applied, why can a picker lift pins indefinitely with no lasting effect?
column2: With no rotational bias, pins float freely in equilibrium under spring force alone; releasing pressure allows springs to return all pins to rest position, since there's no binding/shelf to trap a driver pin above the shear line.

column1: What formula represents the binding order principle, and what does it compute?
column2: Binding Order = argsort_i(r_i × F_shear) — it ranks pin chambers by the torque/moment generated by their radial positional offset, determining which pin binds first, second, etc. under applied tension.

column1: For a 6-pin lock with 9 possible depths per position, what is the theoretical key differ count, and what real-world factor reduces this number?
column2: 9^6 ≈ 530,000 theoretical differs. Maximum Adjacent Cut Specifications (MACS) reduce this space to prevent excessive cut-depth differences between adjacent pins, which would structurally weaken the key blade.

column1: What are the three immutable physical principles underlying all non-destructive bypass (e.g., shimming) methods?
column2: 1) Mechanical systems require clearance for moving parts, creating exploitable gaps. 2) Security and convenience trade off, forcing tolerances that create margins. 3) Many mechanisms rely on a single blocking element whose defeat compromises the whole system.

column1: How does shimming defeat a padlock shackle mechanically, and what dimensional relationship must hold for it to succeed?
column2: A thin shim is inserted into the shackle-body gap to displace the spring-loaded locking pawl from the shackle notch. It succeeds when combined shim thickness exceeds the pawl's engagement depth (1.5–3.0 mm) while staying thin enough to fit the shackle clearance gap (typically 0.20–0.35 mm).

column1: According to ANSI/BHMA A156.5 grading in the lab exercises, what time-to-bypass thresholds distinguish a Grade 1 high-security cylinder from a Commercial Grade 3 cylinder?
column2: Grade 1 (PASS) requires resisting manipulation for ≥10 minutes; Grade 3/needs rework (FAIL) is bypassed in under 2 minutes.
